prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it, which opened the field of moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: Four of the eight openings (mine, Johansson, Mehlig and Danielsson at rank 2) place twisted bilayer graphene high, and I still put it first after reading the others. It is a prediction followed by a decisive experiment: Bistritzer and MacDonald's continuum model gave flat bands at a magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity at that angle. From an electronic-structure viewpoint, a single geometric control parameter tunes a band structure into the strongly correlated regime. That is new physics in a clean, tunable solid, and it has spawned moire physics across graphene multilayers and transition-metal dichalcogenides, many reproduced by independent groups in under a decade. It also fits a short citation that is true to the discovery and not a bundle of loosely related results.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, only about eight years have passed, and sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder complicates some claims. Attribution is also not clean: Eva Andrei's group provided early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities in twisted bilayers, and any three-name set leaves out a serious claimant. If the committee judges the field to be still too fluid, topological insulators (B013) or optical lattice clocks (B006) are the safer, more mature prizes.

responses.point: Johansson also ranks twisted bilayer graphene first but proposes MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Eva Andrei, treating Bistritzer's role as contested.
responses.response: I take Andrei's claim seriously, but I would keep Bistritzer rather than swap him in. The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation is what identified the magic angle and the flat-band condition, and the 2018 experiments were designed around that prediction. Andrei's earlier STM work established that twisted bilayers have renormalized Dirac velocities and van Hove singularities at small angles. That is important evidence but not the prediction or the correlated-phase discovery. I would like the chair's summary to test this ordering. If the committee reads the credit as experiment-led, Andrei could displace Bistritzer, and I would accept that in discussion as a real alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall line (B033) first, as a theory-to-measurement chain and a new classification of matter, with twisted bilayer graphene second but possibly premature.
responses.response: I agree that topological matter is a foundational discovery and that it was my own second choice, so I do not dismiss it. I disagree on two points. B033 bundles the quantum spin Hall effect with the quantum anomalous Hall effect, and the 2016 prize on topological phases already covers part of that ground, which weakens its novelty case. The credited set for B033 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) also omits Mele, who shares the theory credit with Kane. On premature timing, the phenomenology of twisted bilayer graphene is secure and widely reproduced even though the pairing mechanism is open. Earlier prizes have been awarded for an established effect without a settled microscopic explanation.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B006) first as a clean concept-plus-instrument prize: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, Ye's record accuracy, and a pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: The case is strong and I rank it as a serious alternative. Two names, a clear invention, and many independent confirmations make it the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. I put it below twisted bilayer graphene because the physics originality is smaller. It refines well-understood atomic transitions and builds on the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes of 2005 and 2012, whereas twisted bilayer graphene revealed a previously unknown regime of correlated electrons. I would not call clocks inferior, only a different kind of prize, and the committee should choose deliberately between a discovery of new matter and a metrological achievement.

responses.point: Lindroth gives clocks first place and ultracold atoms in optical lattices (B002) second, and sees maturity as a reason clocks are timely rather than premature.
responses.response: I agree that maturity favors clocks, and that is the strongest argument for them against my first choice. I disagree about placing lattice quantum simulation near the top. With five credited names, a three-laureate cap forces an arbitrary exclusion of Esslinger or Cirac, and the headline goals such as the d-wave phase of the fermionic Hubbard model are still unreached. I also see considerable overlap with the earlier cooling and condensate prizes. That makes B002 the weakest of the candidates on attribution.

responses.point: Pearce ranks gamma-ray burst afterglows (B040) first, arguing it is a clean instrument-driven discovery with a mature, overdue record, and ranks IceCube (B008) second.
responses.response: I agree that the afterglow discovery is mature and scientifically decisive, and I place no weight on how far it lies from my own field. My reservation is attribution, which you also note: key people are deceased or not credited, and the optical-follow-up credit is shared between several teams. For IceCube, a single credited name for a very large collaboration is hard to defend. I would rather see a prize with a defensible three-name set than accept an allocation the committee will have to explain away.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept Bistritzer or Andrei as the third laureate alongside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero; I am relying on recall of the historical record, not on verification.
Whether the unresolved superconducting mechanism should delay recognition by a few years.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize and the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize should weigh on B013 and B009, and how much.
I did not form a view on the astrophysical candidates (B040, B008) beyond attribution; I would defer to colleagues with observational expertise.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict with the credited names is apparent from my provided profile. My own work in electronic-structure theory of two-dimensional materials and magnetism is adjacent to twisted bilayer graphene, which is a potential source of bias toward it, so I flag that proximity for colleagues to weigh. I chaired the 2025 committee that awarded the superconducting-circuits prize, which is relevant to how I weigh B009 but is not a recusal matter.
